title: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
summary: Build locks from atomics up: spin locks and cache traffic, when spinning wastes CPU, how FUTEX_WAIT's atomic compare-and-block avoids lost wake-ups, and the three-state futex mutex used by Rust and glibc.
outcomes: Explain why a check-then-set flag fails and how an atomic swap with Acquire and Release makes a correct spin lock
Explain why spinning on loads beats spinning on swap or CAS, and why spinning fails when the holder is preempted
Compute the cost of spin-then-sleep and show that a spin budget equal to the sleep cost is within 2x of optimal
Explain how FUTEX_WAIT's expected value prevents lost wake-ups, and trace the 0/1/2 futex mutex and its syscalls
Choose between spin locks, sleeping mutexes and PI mutexes in user space and in the kernel

lessons.title: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock

blocks.md:
A **critical section** is code that touches shared data and must not run in two threads at once, such as `balance += amount`. A **mutex** (mutual exclusion lock) guarantees that: `lock()` returns in at most one thread at a time, and the others wait until the owner calls `unlock()`.

This course builds locks from the bottom up. From the prerequisites you know that atomic read-modify-write operations like swap and compare-and-swap (CAS) happen indivisibly, and that a system call is a trip into the kernel. Locks are made of exactly those two ingredients.

The obvious first attempt is a boolean flag:

```
while (locked) { }   // wait
locked = true;       // take it
```

It reads well, but it is broken even if every access to `locked` is atomic. Watch two threads run it.

blocks.prompt: Both threads call this lock at nearly the same time while `locked` is false. Can both of them get past it?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The check and the update are **two separate steps**. Thread 2 can load the flag after Thread 1 loaded it but before Thread 1 stored true. Both see false, both store true, and both enter the critical section. Making each access atomic does not help: the *pair* must be atomic.

blocks.title: Two threads, one plain flag, both get in

scenes.caption: The flag starts at false (unlocked). Thread 1 loads it and sees false, so it decides the lock is free.
Before Thread 1 writes anything, Thread 2 loads the same flag. It also sees false.
Both threads now store true and walk into the critical section. The load and the store were two separate steps, and the other thread fit between them.
The fix: one atomic swap that writes true and returns the old value in a single indivisible step. Only the thread that got back false owns the lock.

blocks.md:
A **spin lock** fixes this with one atomic read-modify-write. `swap(true)` stores true and returns the previous value as one indivisible step, so exactly one thread can be the one that turned false into true. Everyone else sees true and tries again, which is called **spinning** or busy-waiting.

Here is the minimal spin lock from Mara Bos's *Rust Atomics and Locks*, chapter 4:

blocks.caption: A minimal spin lock (after Bos, ch. 4). spin_loop() is a CPU hint, covered in the next lesson.

blocks.md: The memory orderings are not decoration. The lock must also make the *data* safe: writes made inside the critical section by the old owner must be visible to the next owner, but the compiler and CPU may otherwise reorder or delay them. The unlock is a **Release** store and the lock is an **Acquire** swap. When the Acquire reads the value written by the Release, everything the old owner did before unlocking **happens-before** (is guaranteed visible to) everything the new owner does after locking. The memory-ordering course covers the full model.
A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

The swap loop is correct but rude to the hardware. Caches keep data in fixed-size blocks called **cache lines**, and a coherence protocol lets many cores hold a read-only copy but only one core hold a writable copy. A swap is a write even when it fails, so each attempt must take the line exclusively, yanking it away from every other core. Bos also notes that on most architectures a *failing* compare-and-exchange claims the line exclusively too.

blocks.title: Where the lock's cache line lives while two cores spin

scenes.caption: Core 0 holds the lock, so its cache has the lock's line in state M (modified, the only copy). Cores 1 and 2 want the lock. Simplified MSI model: real CPUs use MESI or MOESI variants.
Core 1 spins with swap. A swap is a write, so it needs the line in M even though it fails. The line moves from core 0 to core 1: one transfer.
Core 2 swaps too and steals the line from core 1. Every failed attempt drags the line across the chip.
Core 1 tries again: another transfer. The lock holder, which must eventually write the line to unlock, also has to fight for it.
After 4 failed swaps: 4 line transfers, and none of them did useful work.
Now the test-and-test-and-set version, from the same start. Core 1 spins with a plain load. A load only needs a shared copy (S): one transfer.
Core 2 loads as well. Both spinners now hold read-only copies in S. Traffic is 2.
Further loads hit in each core's own cache. The spinners wait quietly and the counter stays at 2 for as long as the lock is held.

Core 0 unlocks with a store: it upgrades its copy to M and the shared copies are invalidated (counted as 3, an invalidation rather than a data transfer). Only now do the spinners reload and race with one swap each.

blocks.md: The standard fix is **test-and-test-and-set**: spin on a plain load until the lock looks free, and only then try the swap. Spinners share a read-only copy and generate no traffic while they wait. Rust's standard library mutex does exactly this in its spin phase; its source comments say it uses only `load` while spinning "to be easier on the caches".

blocks.title: 1 billion relaxed loads of one atomic, reported timings

scenes.caption: Mara Bos's experiment on an older x86-64 machine: a loop of 1 billion loads takes about 300 ms.
A second thread that only loads the same variable changes nothing: both cores keep a shared copy.
A second thread that stores to it makes the loads take about 3 seconds, near 10 times slower. Newer chips show a smaller but still clear gap (reported 250 to 650 ms on a recent AMD).

blocks.md: Atomic does not mean cheap. An atomic write to a line that other cores are reading forces cache-line transfers, and in Bos's measurement it made another core's plain loads about 10 times slower on an older x86-64 machine.

blocks.question: A colleague writes unlock as `locked.store(false, Relaxed)` to save a few cycles. Lock still uses `swap(true, Acquire)`. What can go wrong?
options: The next owner may not see writes made inside the previous critical section
Two threads can own the lock at once
Nothing: Acquire on the lock side is enough
The lock can never be acquired again
blocks.explain: Mutual exclusion still holds, because the swap is atomic regardless of ordering. What breaks is visibility: without a Release store there is no happens-before edge from the old owner's writes to the new owner's reads, so the new owner may read stale data.

blocks.question: Why do good spin locks spin on a load before trying swap or CAS?
options: Loads are atomic and swaps are not
A load puts the thread to sleep in the kernel
A load keeps a shared read-only copy of the cache line, while each swap or CAS needs exclusive ownership of the line
Swap is not allowed while another thread holds the lock
blocks.explain: Every swap or CAS, even a failing one, needs the line in an exclusive state, so spinning with it bounces the line between cores. Loads let all spinners share a copy and stay quiet until the unlock store invalidates it.

lessons.title: When spinning wastes the CPU, and how much to spin

blocks.md: Spinning is a bet that the lock will be free very soon. Bos sums it up: if a lock is held only briefly *and* the waiting threads run in parallel on other cores, spinning can give lower latency than sleeping. Both conditions matter. If the holder is not running, nothing can release the lock, and the spinner is pure waste.

The worst case is **preemption**: the scheduler takes the CPU away from the lock holder because its time slice ran out. In user space a program cannot prevent this. Every thread that then spins on the lock burns CPU time that the holder needed to finish.

blocks.prompt: One CPU, a 4 ms time slice. Thread A's critical section needs 1 ms, but A is preempted 0.5 ms into it; thread B then tries to take the lock. If B spins, when does B get the lock?
blocks.reveal: Not until after its own slice ends. B spins for all 4 ms, A runs again and finishes its remaining 0.5 ms, and B gets the lock at **5.0 ms**. If B had gone to sleep instead, A would have run immediately and B would have the lock at about **1.2 ms** in this model.

blocks.title: One CPU: lock holder preempted while a waiter spins or sleeps

scenes.caption: Model: one CPU and a 4 ms time slice (simplified; real schedulers size slices dynamically). Thread A takes the lock and works for 0.5 ms, then its slice ends while it still holds the lock.
Spin lock: the scheduler runs B, which spins for its whole 4 ms slice. The lock cannot be released, because the only thread that can release it is not running.
Only when B's slice ends does A run again, finish and unlock. B finally gets the lock at 5.0 ms.
Sleeping lock: B finds the lock taken and asks the kernel to put it to sleep (block width not to scale). The CPU goes straight back to A.
A unlocks and wakes B, which gets the lock at 1.2 ms instead of 5.0 ms. Sleeping cost two kernel calls; spinning cost a whole time slice.

blocks.md: The alternative is a **sleeping lock**: a waiter asks the kernel to block it, and the unlocker asks the kernel to wake it. That costs system calls and context switches, but it frees the CPU. Neither choice is always right, so real locks combine them: spin a little, then sleep.

How much is "a little"? Use a simple cost model. Let $W$ be how long the lock stays held after you arrive (unknown in advance) and $C$ the fixed cost of sleeping and being woken. Pure spinning costs $W$. Pure sleeping costs $C$. The best you could do with hindsight is $\min(W, C)$. A strategy that spins for a budget $B$ and then sleeps costs:

blocks.tex: \text{cost}(W) = \begin{cases} W & W \le B \\ B + C & W > B \end{cases} \qquad \text{ratio} = \frac{\text{cost}(W)}{\min(W, C)}

blocks.title: Waiting cost: spin, sleep, or spin then sleep

x.label: time the lock stays held, W

y.label: CPU cost paid by the waiter

params.name: C
params.label: cost of sleeping and waking, C

scenes.caption: Simplified model: spinning burns the whole wait W, sleeping costs a fixed C (system calls plus context switches) no matter how long the wait. Neither wins everywhere.
Spin up to a budget B, then sleep. With B = C = 5, short waits cost exactly W (optimal) and a wait of 8 costs B + C = 10 against a best of 5.
Shrink the budget to B = 2.5: waits just over 2.5 now cost 7.5 where the best is about 2.5, a ratio near 3.
Grow it to B = 10: long waits cost 15 against a best of 5, again 3 times worse. B = C is the sweet spot.

blocks.md: The worst case is a wait just longer than $B$: you paid $B$ spinning and then $C$ to sleep anyway. If $B \le C$ the ratio is $(B + C)/B$; if $B \ge C$ it is $(B + C)/C$. Both equal 2 when $B = C$, and every other budget is worse. This is the classic rent-or-buy argument: spin for about as long as a sleep would cost.

blocks.title: Worst-case ratio as a function of the spin budget

x.label: spin budget as a multiple of C (B / C)

scenes.caption: The worst case of spin-then-sleep is minimized at B = C, where you never pay more than twice the best possible cost, whatever the wait turns out to be.

blocks.md: Real mutexes pick a fixed spin count rather than measuring C. Rust's standard futex mutex spins up to 100 iterations of a relaxed load before sleeping. Bos calls 100 "chosen mostly arbitrarily": the right number depends on the CPU and the cost of a system call.

Inside the spin loop, call a **spin-loop hint**. In Rust that is `std::hint::spin_loop()`, which emits a CPU instruction telling the processor it is busy-waiting (on x86 this is the PAUSE instruction), so it can save power or give a sibling hyper-thread more of the core. It does not talk to the operating system. Its documentation strongly recommends ending a spin loop after a finite number of iterations and making a blocking system call, to avoid problems like priority inversion.
`spin_loop()` is not `yield`. It is a hint to the CPU, not to the scheduler: a thread spinning with it still occupies the CPU for its whole time slice.

blocks.question: Your critical sections take about 50 ns, but the machine runs 32 threads on 8 cores. Should you use a pure spin lock in user space?
options: Yes: 50 ns is shorter than any system call
No: with more threads than cores, holders get preempted, and spinners can then burn whole time slices
Yes, as long as the spin loop calls spin_loop()
No: spin locks do not work with more than 8 threads
blocks.explain: Short critical sections are only half of the condition. With 32 threads on 8 cores the holder is often not running, and a spinner cannot make it run. A spin-then-sleep mutex handles the short case nearly as well and the preempted case far better.

blocks.question: In the cost model, sleeping costs C = 5 units and you spin for a budget B = 5 before sleeping. The lock turns out to be held for W = 3 units. What do you pay?
options: 5 units, because you always sleep eventually
10 units
8 units
3 units: the lock frees up during the spin
blocks.explain: W = 3 is within the budget, so you spin 3 units, take the lock, and never sleep. That equals the best in hindsight, min(3, 5) = 3.

lessons.title: The futex: sleep on an address, wake by address

blocks.md:
To sleep instead of spin, a waiter needs the kernel's help, and the unlocker needs a way to say "wake whoever is waiting for this lock". Older interfaces made *every* lock operation a system call (System V semaphores, `fcntl` locks). The goal of a fast user-space lock is the opposite: lock and unlock with plain atomics in user space, and enter the kernel only when there is contention.

The hard part is the hand-off between the two worlds. A waiter checks the lock, sees it taken, and then asks to sleep. Those are two steps again.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the kernel offered just `sleep()` and `wake_one()`, unrelated to the lock's memory. A waiter checks the lock, sees it held, and calls sleep(). What can go wrong between the check and the sleep?
blocks.reveal: The holder can unlock and call `wake_one()` in that gap. No one is queued yet, so the wake-up is lost. Then the waiter sleeps on a lock that is already free and nobody will wake it. The check and the decision to sleep must be atomic with respect to wake-ups.

scenes.caption: T2 checks the lock word and sees 1 (locked). It decides to go to sleep, but it has not asked the kernel yet.
In that gap T1 unlocks: it stores 0 and asks the kernel to wake a waiter. The kernel's queue is empty, so the wake-up goes to nobody.
Now T2's sleep request arrives. The lock is free, but T2 sleeps anyway, and nobody will ever wake it. This is a lost wake-up.

blocks.md:
A **futex** (fast user-space mutex) solves exactly this. The futex is a 32-bit integer in your memory, called the **futex word**, which must be 4-byte aligned. The `futex()` system call takes its address and an operation. The two core operations:

- `FUTEX_WAIT(uaddr, val)`: if the word at `uaddr` still equals `val`, sleep until woken. Otherwise fail immediately with `EAGAIN`.
- `FUTEX_WAKE(uaddr, n)`: wake at most `n` waiters sleeping on `uaddr` (usually 1 or `INT_MAX`), and return how many were woken.

The man page's key sentence: the load of the futex word, the comparison with the expected value, and starting to sleep "are performed atomically and totally ordered with respect to other futex operations on the same futex word". It calls this an atomic **compare-and-block**, the waiting analogue of compare-and-swap. If the word changed after you decided to sleep, the kernel notices and refuses.

scenes.caption: Same start: T2 loads 1 and decides to wait.
Same race: T1 stores 0 and calls FUTEX_WAKE before T2 is queued. It returns 0 waiters woken.
T2 passes the value it expects, 1. The kernel atomically rereads the word, finds 0, and refuses to sleep: the call fails at once with EAGAIN.
T2 loops back and retries the lock, which now succeeds. The stale decision cost one cheap system call instead of a hang.

blocks.md: FUTEX_WAIT says "sleep only if the word still holds the value I based my decision on". That expected-value check, done atomically by the kernel, is what makes lost wake-ups impossible.

On the kernel side, there is nothing to create or destroy. The kernel keeps internal state for a futex only while someone is waiting on it. The original design by Franke, Russell and Kirkwood (Ottawa Linux Symposium 2002) hashes the word's identity to find a wait queue; for a word in shared memory that identity is the physical page and offset, so two processes can share one futex at different virtual addresses.

blocks.title: Who touches what: user space versus the kernel

scenes.caption: Uncontended: T1 locks with one CAS on a 32-bit word in its own memory. The kernel is not involved and keeps no state for it.
T2 finds it locked and calls FUTEX_WAIT with the word's address. The kernel hashes the address to a bucket and checks the word's value there.
T3 also waits on the same address and joins the same queue. The queue exists only while someone is waiting on that word.
T1 unlocks in user space, then calls FUTEX_WAKE with count 1. The kernel removes one waiter from the queue and makes it runnable; which one is not guaranteed.

blocks.md:
A few facts worth knowing:

- Futex support first merged in Linux 2.5.7 with different semantics; the semantics described here date from 2.5.40.
- `FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG` (Linux 2.6.22) tells the kernel the futex is not shared between processes, which lets it make extra optimizations. The kernel headers provide shorthand constants such as `FUTEX_WAIT_PRIVATE` and `FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE`.
- `FUTEX_WAKE` gives no guarantee about *which* waiter wakes, not even by priority.
- The man page's synopsis calls it through `syscall(SYS_futex, ...)`, as the wrappers below do.

blocks.caption: Thin wrappers over the raw system call, as most futex code uses them.

blocks.md: Returning from FUTEX_WAIT does not mean the lock is yours. The call can fail with EAGAIN, be interrupted by a signal (EINTR), or wake spuriously, and another thread may grab the lock first. Always loop and re-check the word.

blocks.question: A waiter calls `FUTEX_WAIT(&word, 2)`, but by the time the kernel checks, `word` is 0. What happens?
options: The call returns immediately with EAGAIN and the thread does not sleep
The thread sleeps until the next FUTEX_WAKE
The kernel sets the word to 2 and then sleeps
The kernel wakes all other waiters on the word
blocks.explain: FUTEX_WAIT only sleeps if the word equals the expected value at the moment the kernel checks it. A mismatch means the state changed since the caller decided to wait, so it returns EAGAIN and the caller retries in user space.

blocks.question: Why does FUTEX_WAIT take an expected value at all, instead of simply sleeping?
options: To pick which waiter FUTEX_WAKE will wake
To set the futex word to that value before sleeping
So a wake-up that happened after the caller's check but before it was queued is not lost
So the kernel can store the lock state between calls
blocks.explain: The waiter decided to sleep based on an earlier load. If an unlock and wake happened after that load, the word has changed, and the atomic compare in FUTEX_WAIT catches it. The kernel never stores the lock state; it just compares.

lessons.title: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock

blocks.md:
The simplest futex mutex is the spin lock with the spin replaced by a wait. The word is 0 (unlocked) or 1 (locked). Lock does `while swap(1) == 1 { futex_wait(&w, 1) }`. Unlock stores 0 and then calls `futex_wake(&w, 1)`.

It is correct, because the wait's expected value prevents lost wake-ups. But look at unlock: it calls `futex_wake`, a system call, *every time*, even when nobody has ever waited. Most locks in real programs are uncontended most of the time, so this is a tax on the common case.

blocks.prompt: How could unlock know whether anyone might be sleeping, without asking the kernel?
blocks.reveal: Record it in the futex word itself. Split "locked" into two states: **1 = locked, no waiters** and **2 = locked, maybe waiters**. A thread that is about to sleep first sets the word to 2. Unlock then only calls wake if it finds a 2.

blocks.md:
This is the design from Ulrich Drepper's paper *Futexes Are Tricky*, and it is what Rust's standard library uses on Linux today. The three states:

- **0**: unlocked.
- **1**: locked, no other thread waiting.
- **2**: locked, and other threads *may* be waiting.

Lock tries one CAS from 0 to 1. If that fails it swaps in 2 and sleeps with expected value 2 until a swap returns 0. Unlock swaps in 0 and calls wake only if the old value was 2.

blocks.title: Stepping through the three-state lock

scenes.caption: Uncontended lock: the CAS turns 0 into 1 and succeeds. One atomic instruction, no system call.
Uncontended unlock: swap returns 1, not 2, so nobody can be waiting and the wake is skipped.
Contended: T1 holds the lock (s = 1). T2's CAS fails because s is not 0.
T2 swaps in 2 ("locked, maybe waiters") and gets back 1: still locked, so it must wait.
T2 sleeps with expected value 2. If T1 had unlocked in between, s would be 0 and this would return at once.
T1 unlocks. Its swap returns 2, which tells it someone may be sleeping, so it calls futex_wake for one thread.
T2 wakes and loops: swap(2) returns 0, so it now owns the lock. It leaves s at 2 because other sleepers may exist.

blocks.md: Notice that a thread that wakes up locks with `swap(2)`, not by writing 1. Drepper explains why: when it wins, it cannot know whether other threads are still asleep, and guessing wrong would be fatal. So it errs on the safe side and marks the lock contended. The price is an occasional wasted wake call.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the woken thread locked by setting the word to 1 instead of 2, while another thread was still asleep in the kernel. What happens at the next unlock?
blocks.reveal: Unlock's swap returns 1, so it skips `futex_wake`. The sleeping thread is never woken, even though the lock is now free: it can sleep forever. Writing 2 after waking is what keeps the remaining sleepers reachable.

blocks.title: Three threads, one futex word: a full trace

scenes.caption: Start: unlocked (0), nobody waiting, no system calls yet.
T1 locks: CAS 0 to 1 succeeds. Still zero system calls.
T2 arrives: CAS fails, swap(2) returns 1, so T2 calls FUTEX_WAIT(&word, 2) and sleeps.
T3 arrives: CAS fails, swap(2) returns 2, still locked, so it sleeps too. The word stays 2: a third waiter changes nothing.
T1 unlocks: swap(0) returns 2, so it calls FUTEX_WAKE(&word, 1). T2 leaves the queue; the word is 0 for a moment.
T2 runs: swap(2) returns 0, so T2 owns the lock. It must write 2, not 1, because T3 is still asleep.
T2 unlocks: swap returns 2, wake one: T3 leaves the queue.
T3 runs: swap(2) returns 0 and T3 owns the lock, again marking it 2 because it cannot know the queue is empty.
T3 unlocks: swap returns 2, so it calls wake, which finds nobody. Total: 2 waits and 3 wakes, one of them wasted. Run without overlap, the same 3 threads make 0 system calls.

blocks.md: The trace shows the costs precisely. With overlap, the three lock/unlock pairs make **2 waits and 3 wakes**, and the last wake is unnecessary because the queue was already empty. Without overlap, they make **zero** system calls: just one CAS and one swap per pair. Drepper's cost tables give the same verdict: compared with Drepper's simpler first mutex, whose unlock always calls futex_wake, the uncontended unlock trades a system call for an atomic operation, while the contended lock pays extra atomic operations, the price of fixing that first version's bug.

blocks.title: 5 million lock/unlock pairs on one thread, reported

scenes.caption: Bos's uncontended benchmark: the 2-state mutex makes a wake system call on every unlock. About 400 ms on a recent AMD machine, about 1800 ms on an older Intel one.

The 3-state mutex skips the wake when the old state was 1: about 40 ms and 60 ms, so 10x and 30x faster. On macOS both versions took about 50 ms, because its wake function already tracks waiters itself.

blocks.md: A good futex mutex makes the uncontended path pure user space: one CAS to lock, one swap to unlock, zero system calls. The kernel is visited only when a thread really has to sleep, and unlock calls wake only if the word says someone might be sleeping.

Why wake only one thread, not all? Only one waiter can win the lock. Drepper notes that waking 100 waiters would send 99 straight back to sleep, after bouncing the futex word's cache line across every CPU. Waking one is enough, because that thread sets the word to 2 when it takes the lock, so its unlock will wake the next sleeper.

Rust's standard library adds the spin phase from lesson 2 in front of the sleep. In `lock_contended` it first spins up to 100 times with a relaxed load while the state is 1. If the spin ended because the lock is free, it tries one CAS from 0 to 1. Otherwise it enters the swap(2) and wait loop, skipping the swap when the state is already 2 and spinning again after every wake-up. It stops spinning early if it sees 2, since another thread already gave up on spinning.

blocks.caption: The spin phase of Rust's std futex mutex (library/std/src/sys/sync/mutex/futex.rs), lightly trimmed.

blocks.title: 4 threads hammering one lock: does spinning help? (reported)

scenes.caption: Bos's contended benchmark (4 threads, 5 million increments each). On the older Intel machine spinning before sleeping helped: 900 ms to 750 ms.
On the newer AMD machine it hurt: 650 ms to 800 ms. Spinning is a tuning knob whose value depends on hardware and workload, not a free win.

blocks.question: A thread calls lock on an unlocked three-state mutex and later unlocks it, with no other thread involved. How many system calls happen?
options: One: the wake in unlock
Two: a wait and a wake
One: the CAS is a system call
Zero
blocks.explain: The CAS turns 0 into 1 in user space. At unlock the swap returns 1, not 2, so the wake is skipped. Atomic instructions are not system calls; the kernel never sees an uncontended lock.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: `unlock() { if (s.load() == 2) futex_wake(s, 1); s.store(0); }`
options: None: it is equivalent to swap(0) then checking the old value
A thread can set the word to 2 and sleep after the load saw 1, then the store wipes the 2 and no wake ever comes
It wakes too many threads
The store must be Acquire instead of Release
blocks.explain: Reading and resetting must be one atomic swap. If the load sees 1, a waiter may swap in 2 and start sleeping before the store(0). Unlock skipped the wake, the word is now 0, and the sleeper is stranded. Also, waking before unlocking makes the woken thread find the lock still held.

lessons.title: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices

blocks.md: The pattern you built, a fast atomic path plus a bounded spin plus a sleep, is everywhere. Inside the Linux kernel, `struct mutex` keeps the owning task pointer in an atomic `owner` field (NULL when free) and has three acquisition paths, described in the kernel's mutex design document.

blocks.title: The Linux kernel mutex: three ways to acquire

scenes.caption: Fastpath: one cmpxchg swaps the owner field from NULL (0) to the current task pointer. Uncontended locking is a single atomic, just like a futex mutex.
Midpath: if the owner is currently running on another CPU, it will probably release soon, so spin. Spinners line up in an MCS queue so only one competes and each spins on its own cache line.
Slowpath: if the owner is not running or this task needs to reschedule, stop spinning, join the wait queue and sleep until unlock wakes it.

blocks.md: The kernel docs say this optimistic spinning is what makes its mutexes "more practically a hybrid type", and that it significantly improved a number of workloads. The spin condition is smarter than a fixed count: spin only while the owner is actually running on a CPU. That directly addresses lesson 2's failure mode, which user space cannot see as easily.

The kernel also has true **spin locks** (`spinlock_t`, `raw_spinlock_t`), and their rules show when spinning is the only option:

- Spinning locks implicitly **disable preemption** while held, so a holder cannot be scheduled away, which removes the preempted-holder problem.
- Variants such as `spin_lock_irqsave()` also disable interrupts, for data shared with interrupt handlers.
- Sleeping locks (`mutex`, `rw_semaphore`, ...) can only be taken in preemptible task context. An interrupt handler cannot sleep, so it must use a spin lock.

On PREEMPT_RT kernels, `spinlock_t` itself becomes a sleeping lock built on RT-mutexes.

User-space spin locks lack the kernel's guarantee. A user thread cannot disable preemption, so a pure spin lock in an application can always spin against a preempted holder. Prefer the platform mutex, which already spins briefly before sleeping.

**Priority inversion** is the other classic failure. A high-priority task waits for a lock held by a low-priority task, and a medium-priority task keeps preempting the low one, so the lock is never released. The futex man page describes Linux's answer, **priority-inheritance (PI) futexes**: while a high-priority task is blocked on the lock, the holder temporarily runs at that higher priority. PI futexes use a different protocol (`FUTEX_LOCK_PI`, with the owner's thread ID stored in the word) so the kernel knows who to boost.

blocks.prompt: FUTEX_WAKE(&w, 1) wakes thread T2. Before T2 runs, a brand-new thread T4 calls lock on the now-unlocked mutex. With the three-state code, who gets the lock?
blocks.reveal: Most likely **T4**. The word is 0, so T4's fast-path CAS from 0 to 1 succeeds while T2 is still being scheduled. T2 then finds the lock taken, swaps in 2 and sleeps again. This **barging** is allowed by the code and is good for throughput (the lock is never idle while a woken thread wakes up), but it means the lock is not FIFO-fair and a waiter can be overtaken repeatedly.

blocks.md: The futex system call started on Linux, but most systems now have a similar wait and wake on an address. [Bos](https://marabos.nl/atomics/os-primitives.html) lists Windows (`WaitOnAddress`, since Windows 8 in 2012), FreeBSD (`_umtx_op`), and NetBSD and OpenBSD, which have a futex system call of their own. Apple added a public C function, `os_sync_wait_on_address`, in macOS 14.4. On Linux, most programs never call `futex()` directly: glibc's NPTL threads library builds `pthread_mutex_t` and condition variables on it (its internal [lowlevellock.h](https://github.com/bminor/glibc/blob/master/sysdeps/nptl/lowlevellock.h) documents the same 0, 1, and >1 states), and Rust's `std::sync::Mutex` uses the three-state futex lock you just traced.

Choosing a lock: in application code use the standard mutex, which is already uncontended-fast and spin-then-sleep. Reach for a pure spin lock only where the holder cannot be preempted and sections are tiny, as in a kernel with preemption disabled. Reduce contention itself (shorter sections, sharding) before tuning spin counts.

blocks.question: Kernel code running in an interrupt handler needs to protect a counter shared with a normal kernel thread. Which lock fits?
options: struct mutex, because it spins optimistically first
A futex
A spin lock taken with interrupts disabled (for example spin_lock_irqsave) on the thread side
No lock: interrupts cannot run concurrently with threads
blocks.explain: Interrupt handlers cannot sleep, so sleeping locks like mutex are out. The thread side must also disable interrupts while holding the spin lock, or the interrupt could fire on the same CPU and spin forever on a lock its own CPU holds.

blocks.question: A real-time audio thread at high priority sometimes misses deadlines waiting on a mutex held by a low-priority logging thread, while medium-priority work is busy. What directly targets this?
options: Increase the mutex's spin count
Wake all waiters on every unlock
Use a priority-inheritance mutex, such as one built on PI futexes
Switch to FUTEX_PRIVATE_FLAG
blocks.explain: This is priority inversion. With priority inheritance the logging thread temporarily runs at the audio thread's priority while holding the lock, so the medium-priority work cannot starve it. More spinning only burns more CPU at high priority.
